title: Describe a time you had to work with a difficult person: how did you manage the relationship?
shortTitle: Working With a Difficult Person: how did you manage the relationship?
keyPoints: You cannot control their behavior, but you can control your response.
Assume good intent: they are usually optimizing for something you cannot see.
Schedule a one-on-one to understand their perspective before reacting.
Separate the person from the problem: address the behavior, not the character.
Find the shared goal and make the rules objective so the friction becomes neutral.
Build a durable fix (shared definition of done) rather than a one-time patch.
Focus on what YOU did, not on blaming the other person.

s1_definition.oneliner: You cannot control a difficult person's behavior, but you can control your response, find the shared goal, and keep the work moving.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Control your response** – Focus on your own actions, not on changing the other person.
- **Assume good intent** – Most difficult people are optimizing for something you cannot see, not being malicious.
- **One-on-one first** – Understand their perspective before reacting publicly.
- **Shared goal** – Name the common objective out loud so the conflict shrinks.
- **Objective rules** – Replace subjective debates with a written definition of done.
- **Durable fix** – A shared checklist that settles arguments once, not personal mediation every time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine at National Bank of India, Rajesh is a careful backend engineer who wants every edge case tested before release, and a teammate keeps pushing to ship fast. They are both right in their own way, but they keep clashing. Managing a difficult person is like being the bank teller who stays calm with an angry customer: you listen first, find the shared goal, and solve the real problem instead of winning the argument.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Early at National Bank of India I worked closely with a teammate whose style clashed with mine on the transfer service for Rajesh's and Priya's accounts. I wanted full test coverage and a second reviewer on any change that touched customer money, and he wanted to ship quickly. Every code review turned into a personal argument and our pull requests were stuck for days.

Instead of escalating or avoiding him, I asked him for a short one-on-one and listened first. I learned he was under pressure from a commitment he had made to stakeholders, so his urgency was not carelessness, it was a promise. Once I understood that, I separated the person from the problem and proposed something neutral: a shared definition of done. Money-path changes require tests and a second reviewer; everything else can move fast.

After that, the argument disappeared, because the checklist made the decision, not our opinions. Review turnaround dropped from days to hours, and we shipped the feature on time without cutting corners on the money path.

What I learned is that most difficult relationships are really unmanaged expectations. When I assume good intent, find the shared goal, and make the rules objective, the friction usually solves itself and the relationship actually gets stronger.

Remember one sentence: Assume good intent, find the shared goal, and replace subjective friction with an objective written rule that settles the debate permanently.
